source.title: How Narrative Wrapping Affects LLM Refusal: A Cross-Language Benchmark and Defense
source.authors: Zhan-Kai Ye; Yan-Ning Wang; Yu-Kai Jin; Bo Mei; Fang-Yi Li; Wei Wang; Shang-Qian Gao; Xin Liu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies the original difference-in-means representation measure and refusal-direction comparison to new settings, including narrative wrappers, registers, and model variants. It does not reproduce the original all-layer, all-position ablation or steering intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results from its own wrapper, representation, and intervention experiments. Values mentioned only as prior-work results are excluded. The paper's angle and projection analyses are population-level measurements; the authors explicitly describe them as correlational. AXIS's overall method comparisons are not separately catalogued except where the rotation intervention or transfer result bears on a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study applies the Arditi difference-in-means refusal direction to a new setting: narrative-wrapped jailbreaks across English, modern Chinese and Classical Chinese. It reports how far the wrapped harmful–benign contrast turns away from that direction on three models, and that adding the missing projection back along it at inference restores refusal. These results bear on V3, and partly on V1, V5 and V6. It does not reproduce the original all-layer, all-position ablation, so it is T3 rather than T1. The AXIS training results are the study's own defence and bear on no version directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that narrative wrapping, not register, drives jailbreak success. Wrapping leaves harmful and benign requests separable but turns the contrast between them away from the refusal direction, cutting its projection to the benign level. Inference-time fixes fail: angle-only rotation changes nothing, and a constant shift restores refusal but breaks benign answers. AXIS (DPO plus rotation and commitment terms) leads the safety–usability composite, by a margin that shrinks with scale. They call the account correlational and population-level, and say the rotation term's benefit shows the direction is trainable, not causal.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses the last-token harmful-minus-benign mean difference at a selected layer and measures angles and projections relative to a bare-modern-Chinese reference direction. Its interventions are inference-time geometric corrections and a preference-training objective that includes rotation and commitment terms, not the original direction's all-layer, all-position ablation and addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with language/register and wrapper genre; the reported angle also varies by model. Inference-time correction depends on the chosen correction: constant-norm rotation changes nothing, whereas a constant shift restores refusal but harms benign answers. Reported rates vary substantially by judge. AXIS outcomes vary by rotation dose and seed; the paper notes that the 1.7B dose sweep does not reproduce across training runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Training the wrapped harm contrast toward r̂ (AXIS rotation term) closes the angle and raises strict refusal on held-out wrappers (42.8→68.4% at shared dose; +40–47 points at λrot=1), tracking the projection gain (ρ=0.94 at λrot=1; 0.79 at the shared dose). Gains order by the anchor's overlap with r̂.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training the harmful–benign contrast to align with the refusal direction increases refusal of jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: An orthogonal-anchor arm moves the geometry in a direction unrelated to refusal (cosine −0.01 at 9B) yet still refuses. Humans rate it 79.6% vs 81.5% for the real anchor on harm334, a non-significant difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robust refusal can be trained without aligning representations to the diff-in-means refusal direction.

fits_no_version.finding: An AXIS adapter trained only on Classical Chinese refuses 68–74% of the same attacks in modern Chinese and English, against 3.5–9.7% for the untrained model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-level refusal training transfers across registers and languages.

record.problems: The representation account is explicitly correlational and does not predict individual wrapped-request refusals. The authors state that the rotation intervention does not prove causality. The controlled study is centered on one small model family; Qwen3-4B has two seeds and GLM-4-9B one. The single-vendor judge has documented drift and imperfect agreement; human annotations do not cover all larger-model arms. The experiments cover selected benchmarks and a limited language/register range.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted under the 60-row limit. The paper's broad external-method comparison table is not catalogued as separate rows because those methods are not the direction intervention; the specific rotation-term and transfer findings are recorded above.

untested.parts: Directional ablation removing refusal on bare harmful requests. Adding the direction to bare harmless requests. Broad capability evaluation after intervention.
Adversarial training against ablation of the direction. The study tests only the attack side, under narrative wrapping.
No affine, cone or multi-direction model is fitted or compared.
No causal intervention separating the harm representation from the refusal decision.
Base-to-instruct transfer. Behavioural effect of the shared direction across languages (only angles are measured).
Entire version: no comparison of training histories.

missing.what: Per-item refusal projection on r̂ does not predict which wrapped items are refused; the predictive direction is nearly orthogonal to r̂.
Noise floor of the reference direction for bare modern requests: 6–10°. Wrapped direction across ten batches: 81.1° (77–86°).
Best-depth angles: Qwen3-1.7B wrapped 64.8° and bare classical 25.1°; GLM-4-9B 53.4° and 32.0°.
Orthogonal-anchor arm geometry (cosine −0.01) and its refusal rates (harm334 65.4% at 1.7B; human 79.6% vs 81.5%).

record.verdict_notes: The 'base' models in the rows are the released, safety-aligned Qwen3 and GLM-4 checkpoints before the authors' LoRA training, not pretrained base models. The 'instruct' label on R33–R38 is inconsistent with this. The angle rows' 0° baselines ignore the 6–10° noise floor. Judge-dependence (R4–R6) concerns the measurement instrument, not the claim. The study is not an original source of the claim, so all verdicts stand.

versions.untested_parts: No removal of the direction at every layer and position; no direct test that adding it induces refusals to harmless requests. The training intervention is not the original activation ablation or addition. General capability is evaluated on selected benign sets, not broadly.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
The paper measures wrapper-associated changes in direction and attack success, but does not suppress the direction as an attack intervention or train against its ablation.
The paper measures the harmful–benign contrast relative to a refusal direction, but does not test affine, cone, or multi-direction models of refusal.
No direct causal intervention separating a harmfulness representation from a refusal decision; evidence comes from population-level geometry and refusal behavior.

Tests languages/registers and several base-model variants, but not transfer from base to instruct models. The AXIS transfer experiment is a trained defense, not a direct test of an unmodified direction across stages.
Does not compare refusal-training histories or establish when training produces a removable direction.
